messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Shopowner
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun was a 29-year-old South Asian man who owned a small neighborhood shop, a place that kept him busy from early morning until evening and put him in constant contact with customers, delivery drivers, and people passing in and out of the block. A few years earlier, while he was in a relationship, he had been physically abused by his partner in a series of episodes that left him shaken and deeply ashamed. He spoke about the assault in a halting way, but the details that stayed with him were concrete: the suddenness of being grabbed and hurt by someone he had trusted, the closeness of the other person’s body, and the sense that he had been trapped in a moment he could not control or undo. Even now, certain conversation topics could drag him back there without warning, especially when people argued loudly about relationships, loyalty, or what someone “should have done.” He would go quiet in the middle of a discussion, as if he had been pulled away from the room, and then later describe that the memory had come to him all at once, unbidden and complete enough to make his chest tighten and his face burn with anger.

In the months after the abuse, Arjun began to notice how ordinary things could suddenly bring the whole event back. He described moments in the shop when a customer walked in after working out or from the heat outside, carrying the smell of sweat or body odour, and he would instantly feel himself back in the same helpless state, as if the air had changed around him. The reaction was not gradual; it was immediate, and it did not require a clear picture in his mind. Sometimes he would get only the full emotional force of what had happened, a wave of fear and fury with no image attached, leaving him standing behind the counter with his hands clenched and his thoughts racing. At other times, something in his surroundings — a tone of voice, a familiar posture, the sound of someone stepping too close — could flash the memory across him without warning, so vividly that he had to steady himself before he could answer a customer. He said that when the memory came, he often felt intense rage along with it, though the anger did not feel usable or directed anywhere; it just sat in him, hot and humiliating.

Arjun’s sense of safety changed in ways that touched his daily life. He became much more uneasy when strangers approached him, even in ordinary situations, and this was especially noticeable at the shop, where he now watched the doorway more closely than he used to. He found himself scanning people as they came near the counter, trying to decide quickly whether they were too close, too abrupt, or carrying an expression he could not trust. At night, the unease sharpened. He said it was harder to feel safe after dark than during the day, and he often stayed alert long after closing the shop, checking the locks and listening for footsteps in the hallway or outside. Sleep had become difficult; he had trouble falling asleep and often woke during the night, only to lie there awake with his mind on guard and his body refusing to settle. He described this bodily state as if his body kept reacting as though danger were still present, even when he knew, in his rational mind, that he was home and nothing was happening.

Alongside these experiences, Arjun carried a hard judgment about himself. He said he could never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, and this thought came back to him particularly when he remembered the abuse or when he saw other people speaking up for themselves. He spoke as someone who had come to believe he should have reacted differently, should have found a way to prevent the assaults, or should have acted with more force and certainty. That belief sat alongside a deeper loss of confidence in himself more generally: he said he could not rely on himself. He did not trust his own judgment in the same way anymore, and that lack of trust made even small decisions feel weighted. He noticed it in business as well, where he used to feel straightforward and competent, but now second-guessed himself in front of customers or when handling tense interactions. He still managed the shop and maintained his relationship, but he did so with more strain and less ease than before.

Arjun eventually sought help because the pattern had become impossible to ignore. He was tired of feeling braced for impact when a stranger approached, tired of being jolted by smells and conversations that seemed harmless to everyone else, and tired of lying awake at night waiting for his mind to settle. More than anything, he feared that his body and mind would keep reacting as if he were still trapped in that relationship, even though the abuse was over. At the same time, he hoped that therapy might help him feel safe again in his own shop, in his own bed, and in ordinary conversations without the past breaking in so forcefully.
